claims.text: Controlled annealing can induce in situ formation of nanoscale precipitates in a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The annealing-induced precipitates will be non-magnetic and may be Cr-rich.
Formation of these precipitates will increase coercive field relative to the as-cast single-phase state.
The proposed baseline is a homogeneous, single-phase magnetic HEA with a disordered BCC or FCC structure.
The baseline has minimal inherent precipitate formation.
Annealing at a selected subcritical temperature and duration will induce limited phase segregation.
Limited phase segregation will produce nanoscale Cr-rich or similarly non-magnetic precipitates.
Tuning annealing temperature and time can retain precipitate sizes in the 3–5 nm range while maintaining the overall crystal structure.
The nanoscale precipitates will occur at grain boundaries or within grains.
The nanoscale precipitates act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Precipitate pinning impedes magnetic domain-wall motion under an applied field.
Increased domain-wall pinning increases the coercive field.
The annealed material should have a higher coercive field than an otherwise composition-matched as-cast material.
The coercivity benefit is expected only while precipitates remain within an optimal nanometer-scale size range.
Coarsened precipitates will be less effective at increasing coercivity.
Excessive phase separation or degradation of the primary magnetic phase could negate the coercivity benefit.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase is specified as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the effect is expected only when the target nanoscale precipitate morphology is achieved, but the falsification rule says that failure to achieve that morphology itself refutes the hypothesis. Failure of the intervention to create the stipulated mediator tests treatment execution, not the conditional causal hypothesis.
